E1627.summary: Cited authority (Eccles.) whom Atwood uses to show that Wisdom first tries her follower with fear before revealing her Secret.
E1627.body: Cited by Atwood (Eccles. 1:20; 4:17, 18, 28) in support of the point that Wisdom first tries a man with fear and only then reveals her Secret: “at first she will walk with him by crooked ways, and bring fear and dread upon him” [II.3 ¶37; II.3 n43]. Atwood attributes this to the same intimate experience she is describing, and uses it approvingly.

E1629.summary: Basil's name for practitioners of the Art, who all aim at the 'harbor' reached when the Matter's bonds are loosed after its due time.
E1629.body: In a passage quoted from Basil, the sons of Art are the practitioners of the Art, whose common goal is the loosing of the Matter's bonds after its due time: “loose its bonds towards which all sons of Art aim to arrive as to their long-desired and sought for harbor” [IV.1 ¶15].

E1630.summary: In Atwood's Table Talk, that which alchemy seeks in the mind.
E1630.body: Atwood speaks of alchemy as “the seeking of The Sophia in the mind” [APP ¶183] (Appendix, Table Talk, a later layer). The text gives no further definition here.

E1631.summary: Cited by Atwood to illustrate the same point: that life is to be had only there, all other places being full of misery and evil.
E1631.body: Cited by Atwood as illustrating the same point as the surrounding passage: “Life only is to be had there, all other places are full of misery and evil” [II.2 ¶5; II.2 n8].

E1632.summary: In Atwood's Table Talk, the soul is the body's ultimate perfection, a mesothesis between two spheres, and in its metalline perfection the philosopher's stone.
E1632.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood writes: “The human soul is more than a mere resultant of body; it is its ultimate perfection, for it is a mesothesis between two spheres.” [APP ¶178]. Its angelic essence is described as a metallic humidity, and she identifies the perfected soul with the philosopher's stone: “The soul in its metalline perfection is the philosopher’s stone.” [APP ¶181].

E1633.summary: In Sendivogius as quoted, what man possesses and other creatures, which have only spirit, lack.
E1633.body: Sendivogius, as quoted, distinguishes man from other creatures, which “have only spirit and not the soul of Deity” [II.1 ¶10]; man alone has the soul of Deity.

E1634.summary: An ingredient in Hermes' recipe, identified with the Meridian Redness and, by the Scholiast, with the true aurific principle that perfects the seven bodies.
E1634.body: In Hermes' recipe as quoted, the soul of gold is one ingredient, identified with the Meridian Redness: “the Meridian Redness, that is the soul of gold” [I.3 ¶6]. The Scholiast, who reads the whole recipe as a matter of distillation, explains it as “our soul of gold, writes the Scholiast, which is the true aurific principle” [I.3 n65]: a medium that perfects the seven bodies as the sun perfects sublunary nature.

E1635.summary: Works in which, Atwood says, the adepts esoterically credit prayer with efficacy when the mind is lifted up; not further defined.
E1635.body: Atwood notes that “adepts are eloquent in their imputations of its efficacy in Spagyric Works, when the mind is lifted up” [III.4 ¶22], referring to prayer. The text does not define Spagyric Works further.

E1636.summary: The specific kind of a thing (lead as lead); indestructible and not transmutable, contrasted with the Universal Subject to which transmutation actually relates.
E1636.body: Atwood uses species in a special sense: the specific kind of a thing, as lead considered as lead. Species are indestructible, not liable to corruption and not transmutable: “It is not species that they profess to transmute” [I.2 ¶4]. Transmutation instead concerns what underlies them, “relating not to Species but to their Universal Subject” [IV.4 ¶2].

E1637.summary: Contemplation in which, according to Proclus, the same order holds as in the Mysteries: phantasms first, illumination afterwards.
E1637.body: Proclus, as quoted, says that “the same method takes place in the speculation of Wholes” [II.3 ¶22] as in the Mysteries: phantasms appear first and illumination comes later.

E1638.summary: In Pierce the Black Monk's verse, a seed taken out of a body that contains all things, set against common gold and silver.
E1638.body: In verse quoted from Pierce, the Black Monk, the sperme is a seed drawn from a body, set against common gold and silver: “But a sperme owte of a body I take,” [III.4 ¶21]. It contains all: “In the which is alle, Sol, Lune, Life and Light, Water and Erth, Fyre and Fryght:” [III.4 ¶21].

E1639.summary: Atwood's figure for the Ether, Door-keeper of the Egyptian Mysteries, whose enigma must be fully solved lest she regain dominion over the work.
E1639.body:
Atwood says the Egyptians placed the Sphinx in the vestibule of Isis, and identifies her with the Ether: “so is that Ether then the Sphinx of the Universe” [III.1 ¶5]; “Such was the Door-keeper of the Egyptian Mysteries” [III.1 ¶6]. She is the passive counterpart of the inner light: “And she is all things passively which the internal light is impassively.” [III.1 ¶6]. Her animal form with a human face shows a twofold life, and her 'winds' image the elevating power of imagination; the ancients mastered her [III.1 ¶6].

In the practice, the Sphinx is a power that must be fully overcome: if the dissolution is left incomplete before the total solution of her enigma, “the Sphinx should retrieve her dominion unawares and frustrate the work begun” [IV.1 ¶7].

E1640.summary: The fabled Sphinx, cited as the barrier at the vestibule admitting only philosophers, whose riddle Oedipus solved.
E1640.body: Atwood cites the Sphinx as the barrier at the vestibule that perplexes intruders and admits only philosophers [IV.4 ¶5]. She uses Oedipus' solving of the riddle to illustrate the rational penetration of one's own natural understanding: one who, “like Oedipus, is able to solve the Enigma of the Sphinx” [IV.1 ¶48]. See also the term Sphinx.

E1641.summary: Fables cited by Atwood to illustrate the reduction to a simple estate of Being.
E1641.body: Atwood cites these fables to illustrate the reduction to a simple estate of Being, with the image of something “carried within the temple upon the back of an ass” [III.2 ¶64].

E1642.summary: Atwood's figure for that to which her preceding exposition has served as introduction; not explained.
E1642.body: Atwood closes a section: “we conclude our introduction, as it may be called, to the Sphinx’s lair” [III.4 ¶47]. The figure is not explained.

E1643.summary: Named by Atwood as a metaphysician who speculated on the same experimental ground.
E1643.body: Atwood names Spinoza among metaphysicians and speculators on the same experimental ground [I.1 ¶39]; the text says nothing further about him.

E1644.summary: The life-principle of the matter, whose association sums up the Art; in the work it wakes, unifies, builds its own vessel, and (per Eudoxus) is the tie of soul and body, called Eve and Mercury.
E1644.body:
**In the work.** The Spirit's removal is the matter's death and its return is its life; it must be kept from escaping the vessel: “In the life and death thereof we work with the spirits” [I.3 ¶49]. The Art is summed up in it: “In a scientific association of the Spirit the Hermetic Art has been said summarily to consist” [I.3 n59]. Atwood also speaks of its superior life, its two invisible poles and its external forms (voice partly unclear in these records).

**Atwood's account.** The Spirit wakes in the congress of allied mind: “the Spirit wakes to consciousness” [III.4 ¶27]; “these diversified parts of the Spirit are in the renascent harmony made one” [III.4 ¶28]. It cannot increase without a medium and a bond. “The Spirit finally constructs its own vessel and vitrifies it” [III.4 ¶32], and it tests the instruments, “as by the Spirit they are proved fit” [III.4 ¶40].

**The Zohar.** The Rabbi in the Zohar, as quoted: “When the Thought begins to develop itself forth, it arrives at that degree when it becomes Spirit.” At this point it is no longer shut up in itself: “Arrived at this estate, it takes the name of Intelligence” [III.3 ¶78].

**Eudoxus.** Joined with body to form the Stone, the Spirit is the soul and body's only tie, “of whom the Spirit is the only tie which works this conjunction”, and is used to wash the earth; “the Spirit is Eve, the Body is Adam” [IV.3 ¶7]. It is “the Spirit, which is our Mercury” [IV.3 ¶12]. It is corporified (turned to earth) in the Fourth Key, and in the Fifth it unites paste and leaven. In the plural, the spirits of the bodies are the Bath and unite permanently with purified bodies: “the spirits desire to be in the cleansed bodies, and having them, they enliven and dwell in them” [IV.3 ¶10].

E1645.summary: In Atwood's Table Talk, nature's spirit is all imagination, realizing its imaginings in aromal essences; literal chemists vainly hoped to sublime it with lifeless instruments.
E1645.body:
In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood writes: “The spirit of nature is all imagination, ideality, fancy.” [APP ¶122]. It wraps itself in aromal essences to realize its imaginings. It is a personality in particulars, and “when regarded universally it is the same in the being of the orb soul” [APP ¶122]; it grows more phantastic the more power it is given from the Central Source.

In the main text she criticizes literal chemists who worked with stills and furnaces “in hope by such lifeless instruments to sublime the Spirit of Nature” [I.1 ¶86], implying that such instruments cannot do it.

E1646.summary: In the Apostle's words as quoted, the Spirit that brings liberty and changes its beholders into the same image; identified with the Lord.
E1646.body: The Apostle, as quoted: where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty, and its beholders are changed into the same image, “even as by the Spirit of the Lord” [III.3 ¶59]. It is identified with the Lord: “For the Lord is that Spirit” [III.3 ¶59].

E1647.summary: Spirit in its natural state, which Atwood calls degraded and incapable of true intelligence: diseased, falsifying and dulled until clarified.
E1647.body: Atwood reports the condemnation of “the Spirit of the natural life as degraded and incapable of true intelligence” [II.2 ¶8], and asks “in what the disease of the Spirit consists” [II.2 ¶9]. In this state the spirit is diseased, falsifying and dulled until it is clarified.

E1648.summary: A vindicative power upholding Wisdom's Rule, fulfilling it lovingly but confounding whoever abandons the Divine purpose for private ends.
E1648.body: Atwood writes of “the vindicative Spirit of Wisdom for the justification of her Rule” [IV.3 ¶56]. “The Spirit of Wisdom runs lovingly by her own Rule to fulfill it” [IV.3 ¶56], but leaves in confusion whoever turns from the Divine purpose to private ends.

E1649.summary: The Spirit's words to Dr Dee (Dee’s Conversat.), cited by Atwood in support of steadfastly continuing the labor to its end.
E1649.body: Atwood cites the Spirit's words to Dr Dee (Dee’s Conversat.) in support of continuing the labor steadfastly to the end: “to fight against the Powers of Darkness requires great force” [IV.1 ¶7; IV.1 n8].

E1650.summary: In Atwood's Table Talk, the spiritual man within the natural man, whose work is to move the Ether.
E1650.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer): “There is a spirit-man within the natural man” [APP ¶139]; its work is to move the Ether.

E1651.summary: In Atwood's Table Talk, promptings from spirits, which give the spirits footing in the life when uttered.
E1651.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood warns: “To utter from spirit-suggestions is a fearful thing” [APP ¶127], because doing so gives the spirits footing in the life.

E1652.summary: The work's two principles, active and receptive: equal Spirits that must both be prepared and allied, each dying in the other so their reunion yields new life.
E1652.body: Atwood names the two principles of the work, active and receptive, as equal Spirits that must both be made ready and brought together: “Both therefore have to be prepared --- the spiritual agent and the spiritual patient” [III.1 ¶41]. Each dies in the other, “by death and contrition of the agent in the patient, and vice versa” [III.1 ¶49]. The old life is crucified, and their reunion under another law brings forth the new life.

E1653.summary: Fermentation performed by multiplying the tinctures, not by using common gold or silver.
E1653.body: Atwood: “The spiritual fermentation is performed by multiplying the tinctures” [IV.3 ¶21], and not with common gold or silver.

E1654.summary: Generation under the law that the parent is bettered in the offspring, up to a fourth or fifth generation.
E1654.body: Atwood states “the Law especial of spiritual generation that the parent is bettered in the offspring” [III.1 ¶30], up to a fourth or fifth generation.

E1655.summary: The one whose constitution and instinct determine how the conditions of the work vary; not further defined.
E1655.body: Atwood says that the work's conditions are those “which vary with the constitution and instinct of the spiritual guide” [III.4 ¶42]. The text does not define the spiritual guide further here.

E1656.summary: The intellect which natural reason helps bring into self-knowledge, and which then turns back on the outer life to analyze and transform it.
E1656.body: Atwood describes natural reason as helping to introduce the spiritual intellect into self-knowledge. Once there, “this latter, returning with power upon the life without, proceeds to analyze and revolutionize” [III.1 ¶13] that outer life 'chemically'. The phrase that follows, 'this vital perscrutinator' (the operating agent of the change), apparently refers to this same intellect.

E1657.summary: In St. Paul's words as quoted, the rock that followed the Fathers and gave them spiritual drink, identified with Christ.
E1657.body: St. Paul, as quoted, says the Fathers drank spiritual drink: “they drank of that spiritual rock that followed them” and “and that rock was Christ” [III.3 ¶59].
